title: Development of novel minimally-invasive methods to determine the risk of progression for patients with smoldering multiple myeloma via longitudinal characterization of tumor cells and immune cells
summary:
Multiple myeloma (MM) is a plasma cell malignancy with a median survival of about one year without treatment. In recent years, high-dose chemotherapy with ensuing autologous stem cell transplant and the use of novel substances and monoclonal antibodies has greatly improved the outlook for patients. However, most patients progress after a period of remission, and will become refractory. MM is therefore still considered incurable.  
Smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM), a precursor stage to MM, progresses to a treatment necessitating MM with a probability of 10% per year in the first five years after first diagnosis. Several studies showed that SMM-patients with a high risk of progression benefit from early treatment intervention. However, risk of progression is varied in SMM. Via clinical parameters and biomarkers, high risk groups may be identified. However, an adequate assessment as yet is still not satisfactorily possible and the mechanisms underlying progression are all but known. 
The aim of the current study is to better understand the progression of SMM to MM and to develop minimally-invasive methods based on this newly gained insight, which will allow an adequate risk prediction. A total of 100 SMM-patients is to be surveilled longitudinally over the course of 3 years. At predefined timepoints, peripheral blood and bone-marrow will be collected at routine visits, in order to define the epigenome, the transcriptome and protein profile of tumor cells longitudinally via single-cell analyses and flowcytometry and to identify those immunosignatures which correlate with risk of progression. As an additional potentially significant biomarker, the mutational burden of circulating free DNA and the amount of exosomal micro-RNA will be analyzed. 
The long-term goal of this study is to effectively identify those SMM-patients with a high risk of progression and to offer them early treatment so as to prevent the transition to MM necessitating treatment in order to enable a cure.

Inclusion criteria:
Patients with diagnosed SMM, which have presented at the Heidelberg University Hospital
